Security deposit rules

A Colorado landlord can hold no more than two months of rent as a security deposit, under C.R.S. 38-12-102.5. A few related limits go with it:

  • An extra pet deposit cannot be more than $300, and it must be refundable.
  • The landlord may deduct for unpaid rent, abandonment, unpaid utilities and repair or cleaning the tenant agreed to pay. Normal wear and tear is off limits.
  • A landlord who keeps any of the deposit must send a written statement giving the exact reasons and refund the rest. Missing the deadline forfeits the right to withhold anything.
  • A tenant cannot waive deposit rights, and a lease clause that tries to do so is unenforceable.

What happens to the deposit when the landlord sells

The deposit travels with the property. Under C.R.S. 38-12-103(4), when a rental changes hands the deposit goes to the new owner, or it goes back to the tenant after lawful deductions. The rule covers any change in ownership, including sale, assignment, death or receivership. An owner who sells a rented house cannot pocket the tenant's deposit and walk away.

That leaves two paths at closing:

  1. Hand the deposit to the buyer and write the amount into the sale contract so both sides agree on it.
  2. Return it to the tenant, with a written itemization of any deductions, if the tenant is leaving.

Tell the title company which path you are taking so the settlement statement shows the deposit correctly.

Warranty of habitability

Every Colorado landlord warrants that a rental is fit to live in and must keep it that way for the whole tenancy. The warranty is in C.R.S. 38-12-503(1) and runs through the Part 5 statutes, which the legislature updated in 2024.

A breach has three parts: an uninhabitable condition, notice to the landlord, and a failure to begin or finish repairs. The statute sorts problems into two groups.

GroupExamples in the statute
Regular conditionsMold that materially affects health or safety, a substantial lack of working appliances, plumbing or gas not maintained, electrical systems not maintained, code violations
Conditions that materially interfere with life, health or safetyGas hazards, inadequate running or hot water, no electricity or hazardous wiring, no working exterior locks, rodent, pest or insect infestations

Tenants have duties too. They must keep the unit clean, safe and habitable, and a landlord is not responsible for problems the tenant caused through action, inaction or negligence.

How fast a landlord must respond to a repair notice

For a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety, remedial action has to start within 24 hours of notice, under C.R.S. 38-12-503(2)(b). If the tenant asks, the landlord must also supply a comparable unit or a hotel room at no cost within 24 hours of the request. The landlord is presumed to have failed when such a condition persists seven calendar days after notice.

Work must continue until the problem is fully fixed within a reasonable time. The landlord has a defense when the tenant caused the delay by denying entry, refusing a reasonable alternative time or otherwise slowing the repairs.

If you may sell the rental, keep dated records of every repair notice and every response. A buyer will ask to see them.

What a tenant can do when repairs are not made

C.R.S. 38-12-507 lists several remedies.

  • Terminate the lease. If a condition is still unfixed after a reasonable time, the tenant can end the lease with 10 to 60 days of written notice, with a termination date at least 10 days out.
  • Terminate for a repeat problem. If the same condition returns within six months of being fixed, 10 days of written notice is enough.
  • Deduct repair costs from rent. This takes 10 days of written notice, or 48 hours for conditions that materially interfere with health or safety, plus a qualified professional and a chance for the landlord to fix it first.
  • Go to court. Actual and punitive damages, costs, reasonable attorney fees, injunctions, restraining orders and specific performance are all listed.

An owner planning to sell usually wants repairs finished before the first showing, not after a tenant has started down one of these paths.

Landlord retaliation

A landlord may not punish a tenant for using habitability rights. Section 38-12-509 protects tenants who raise problems with the landlord, a third party or a government agency, or who join a tenants' organization. Retaliatory acts include:

  • Raising rent or decreasing services.
  • Ending or declining to renew a lease without the tenant's written consent.
  • Starting or threatening an eviction.
  • Charging a fee, cost or penalty.
  • Intimidation, threats, discrimination or harassment.

A tenant who proves retaliation can recover damages, attorney fees and costs, and may end the lease. Retaliation can also be raised as a defense in a possession case. The statute does not stop a landlord from serving a notice to terminate or vacate where Colorado law allows one.

Timing is the lesson for a seller. A termination notice served right after a repair complaint invites a retaliation argument.

Does a landlord need a reason to end a tenancy?

Yes. House Bill 24-1098 and C.R.S. 38-12-1303 require cause before a landlord serves a notice to terminate or files a possession action. As of November 2024 the legislature's summary counted 13 for-cause situations, including holding over after the lease ends, nonpayment, material lease violations and nuisance or negligent damage.

No-fault reasons are separate. One is that the landlord intends to stop renting and sell the home. The JDF 99 C form requires at least 90 days of notice for that route, with a move-out date after the lease term ends.

The form excludes tenants who have lived in the home less than a year, resident landlords of a single-family home, duplex or triplex, employer-provided housing, mobile home spaces and short-term rentals. Our eviction process page covers how those cases move through court.

Whether a buyer takes the house with a tenancy in place depends on the sale contract, the lease and these notice rules.

Selling a rental house for cash

A rental can be sold as is, with the tenant in place or after a lawful move-out. The law mostly decides how a tenancy ends, not whether the owner can sell.

Gather these items before you talk to a buyer:

  • The lease and any amendments.
  • The deposit amount and where it is held.
  • Written repair requests and records of what was done.
  • Any notice already served and the date it was served.

With those in hand, a buyer can price the house and the closing can be built around the tenant's situation. A buyer who takes the house occupied inherits the lease, so the lease terms, the rent and the deposit all belong in the contract. A buyer who wants it empty will need a lawful move-out first, and that sets the closing date.

We buy houses in Colorado as is, and we can walk through your lease and dates before you decide on a path. For legal questions, a Colorado attorney is the right call.

Frequently asked questions

How much can a Colorado landlord charge for a security deposit?

No more than two months of rent. An additional pet deposit is limited to $300 and must be refundable.

What happens to the tenant's deposit if I sell the rental?

It must be given to the new owner or returned to the tenant after lawful deductions. The rule covers sale, assignment, death and receivership.

How quickly must a landlord start repairs on a dangerous condition?

Within 24 hours of notice for conditions that materially interfere with life, health or safety, such as gas hazards or no working exterior locks.

Can a tenant withhold rent for repairs?

Only by following the statute: 10 days of written notice, or 48 hours for health and safety conditions, using a qualified professional and giving the landlord a chance to fix it first.

Can I end a tenancy because I want to sell?

Yes, through the no-fault route, with at least 90 days of notice on form JDF 99 C. Tenants who have lived there less than a year and certain other groups are not covered by that form.

Where a Colorado eviction case is filed

Evictions go through the state court system. Colorado has 23 judicial districts, and each has a district court and a county court with limited jurisdiction. A residential eviction case lands in the county where the rental house sits, so a landlord who owns houses in two counties may end up with two cases in two courts, each with its own clerk.

The Colorado Judicial Branch runs a Residential Evictions self-help page that sorts its material into guides, step-by-step forms, subpoenas, frequently asked questions and extra resources. The forms for house, apartment and condo evictions are gathered in one place there. A landlord or tenant who cannot afford the filing fee can ask to file without paying, and the Court Resource Centers can point people to help.

Before anything is filed, there is a notice. The type you serve depends on why the tenancy is ending, and it sets the clock for everything that follows. A wrong or late notice usually means starting over, so confirm the form and the deadline with the court or an attorney before you serve it.

Unlawful eviction by a landlord

Changing the locks, shutting off utilities or carting away belongings is a fast way to end up as the defendant. The Judicial Branch's guidance on unlawful evictions says landlords must follow the right process, and a tenant whose landlord skips it can file a lawsuit.

A tenant who wins can get two kinds of relief:

  • Money from the court, called damages.
  • An injunction from a district court, which stops the unlawful eviction while the case is pending.

An owner who plans to sell a rented house gets no shortcut from the sale. The tenancy continues until it is ended through the court process, and a pending sale contract does not change that.

How the tenant's lawsuit moves

The forms for an unlawful eviction suit follow a five step order. The deadline for the landlord's answer depends on which court the case is in.

StepWhat happensForms or timing
1Tenant starts the caseComplaint, JDF 601 cover sheet for district court, Form 1 summons for county court or JDF 600 for district court
2Tenant serves the landlordJDF 98 Affidavit of Service
3Landlord respondsDue within 14 days in county court, 21 days in district court
4Hearing preparationJDF 71 witness list, JDF 72 exhibit list, subpoena forms
5As neededJDF 205 motion to waive the filing fee; restraining order motion in district court

The restraining order motion has no standard form, and it belongs to the district court process only.

If you are the landlord and you get served, do not let the answer date slide. A missed deadline in a case like this hands the other side an easy win, and a sale that was already in motion can stall while you sort it out.

Choosing the right notice before you sell

Your choice of notice drives how long you wait and whether the buyer gets a vacant house. Match it to the real reason you are ending the tenancy, and serve it the way the court forms describe.

An owner who wants to sell has a few paths:

  • Serve the notice that fits the situation, then sell after the tenant leaves.
  • Sell the house with the tenant still in it, to a buyer who agrees to take it that way.
  • Agree on a move-out date with the tenant in writing.
  • Sell for cash as is and let the buyer handle the occupancy question.

Each path costs something in time. A buyer who needs a vacant house waits for the tenant to leave. A buyer who accepts an occupied house does not.

A written agreement with the tenant is often the cleanest option, because it can set the move-out date, the condition of the house and what happens to the deposit without a court case. Keep a copy, and give the buyer a copy of the lease and any notices that were served.

Taxes when you sell a rental house

A house that was never your residence does not qualify for the home sale exclusion. That exclusion covers up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, and only for a main home that passes both the ownership and use tests, each of which needs 24 months in the five years before the sale.

Colorado follows the federal figure. Income from real property in the state, capital gains included, counts as Colorado source income. A landlord who lives out of state will usually see the closing agent withhold 2 percent of the sale price or the net proceeds, whichever is less, and the landlord claims that amount on a Colorado return.

If you did live in the house at some point, part of the exclusion may still apply. Ask a tax professional before you decide how to price or time the sale.

Reporting the sale

Expect paperwork even when the gain is small. If you receive a Form 1099-S, the sale goes on your return even if the gain is excludable, and it must be reported whenever you cannot exclude all of it. Schedule D and Form 8949 are the usual places to report it.

Colorado adds its own return. Nonresidents with Colorado source income file a Colorado return when they have to file a federal return or when they owe Colorado tax. Withholding at closing is claimed on the line for form DR 1079, not the W-2 or 1099 line, and a refund comes back if the amount withheld is more than the tax owed.

Keep the closing statement, the lease, repair invoices and any insurance claim paperwork in one folder. If a tenant dispute turns on repairs, dated photos and records of what the tenant reported, and when, carry more weight than memory does.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Colorado houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Paperwork to pull together first

Whichever route you choose, a short folder of documents saves days later. Gather the signed lease, the record of rent paid and unpaid, copies of every notice you served along with proof of how and when it was delivered, and any filings if a case has already started. If a tenant raised repair complaints, add the dated requests and what was done about each one.

With that folder, a buyer or the title company can see the real status of the tenancy at a glance. Without it, questions pile up at closing and the date can slip. If a case is already filed, give the buyer the case number and the hearing date so the contract can be timed around them.

Problems landlords run into when selling

Three things slow most rental sales: a tenant who stops paying, a lease that runs past the date you wanted to close, and a house that needs work. A standard listing suffers from each, because lenders and buyers generally want a vacant, move-in ready home.

A cash sale as is removes several of those obstacles. We buy houses in Colorado in their current condition, including rentals with tenants in them, and we can talk through the notice timeline with you before you commit to anything.

This page is general information and not legal advice, so confirm forms and deadlines with the court or a Colorado attorney.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Colorado tenant sue a landlord for an unlawful eviction?

Yes. If a landlord skips the legal process, the tenant can file a lawsuit and may be awarded damages.

How long does a landlord have to answer a tenant's unlawful eviction case?

The response is due within 14 days in county court and 21 days in district court.

Where do I find Colorado eviction forms?

The Colorado Judicial Branch gathers the forms for house, apartment and condo evictions on its Residential Evictions self-help page.

Can I sell a house with a tenant in it in Colorado?

Yes, but the tenancy continues until it is lawfully ended. A buyer who will take the house occupied, or a cash buyer, is usually the fastest route.

Is the gain on a rental house sale taxable in Colorado?

It can be. A house you never lived in does not meet the federal use test, and Colorado treats gain from Colorado real property as Colorado source income.
